ref: 1.10.1 (Stieren/Massuet numbering used by Harvey and ANF); Harvey's Latin heading for the passage: 'Expositio praedicationis veritatis, quam ab Apostolis Ecclesia percipiens custodit'
greek: Ἡ μὲν γὰρ Ἐκκλησία, καίπερ καθ᾽ ὅλης τῆς οἰκουμένης ἕως περάτων τῆς γῆς διεσπαρμένη, παρὰ δὲ τῶν Ἀποστόλων, καὶ τῶν ἐκείνων μαθητῶν παραλαβοῦσα τὴν εἰς ἕνα Θεὸν Πατέρα παντοκράτορα, τὸν πεποιηκότα τὸν οὐρανὸν, καὶ τὴν γῆν, καὶ τὰς θαλάσσας, καὶ πάντα τὰ ἐν αὐτοῖς, πίστιν· καὶ εἰς ἕνα Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν, τὸν Υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, τὸν σαρκωθέντα ὑπὲρ τῆς ἡμετέρας σωτηρίας· καὶ εἰς Πνεῦμα ἅγιον, τὸ διὰ τῶν Προφητῶν κεκηρυχὸς τὰς οἰκονομίας, καὶ τὰς ἐλεύσεις
greek_edition: Greek of 1.10.1 (quoted from Epiphanius) read from Harvey 1857 vol. 1 p. 90 (PDF p. 289) by Tesseract OCR of the page image, and independently from the Migne PG 7 djvu OCR (Greek, 'Ἡ μὲν γὰρ Ἐκκλησία', section 1; column not read). Both are OCR: accents and breathings are NOT proofed against a print edition; re-copy from a scan before use.
english: The Church, though dispersed throughout the whole world, even to the ends of the earth, has received from the apostles and their disciples this faith: in one God, the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are in them; and in one Christ Jesus, the Son of God, who became incarnate for our salvation (ANF text layer, p. 330; see I9-03)
translator: English: W. H. Rambaut (groundwork), revised under Alexander Roberts, ANF vol. 1
page: Harvey 1857 vol.1 p. 90 (running head REGULA); Migne PG 7 column not read
edition: Sancti Irenaei ... libros quinque adversus haereses, ed. W. Wigan Harvey, vol. 1, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (archive.org sanctiirenilibr01irengoog; image PDF, OCR only); Migne PG 7 (1857), archive.org djvu text
what_it_says: The Church, dispersed through the world, holds one faith in one God the Father Almighty, in one Christ Jesus the Son of God, and in the Holy Spirit: the rule that Irenaeus sets against Valentinian multiplication of the Christ.
limits: The rule names the Father, the Son and the Spirit but does not define the Son's or Spirit's consubstantiality; it is a creed-shaped summary and does not answer Arian questions by itself. Greek survives only as Epiphanian citation (Greek in this passage is partial).

ref: 1.10.1 (ANF section 1, 'UNITY OF THE FAITH OF THE CHURCH THROUGHOUT THE WHOLE WORLD')
english: The Church, though dispersed throughout the whole world, even to the ends of the earth, has received from the apostles and their disciples this faith: [She believes] in one God, the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are in them; and in one Christ Jesus, the Son of God, who became incarnate for our salvation; and in the Holy Spirit, who proclaimed through the prophets the dispensations of God
translator: English: W. H. Rambaut (groundwork), revised under Alexander Roberts, ANF vol. 1
page: ANF p. 330 (PDF p. 348; printed page from running-head offset 18, consistent on pdf 335-585, and ANF index lists 'unity of the faith ... 330')
edition: The Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1 (ed. Roberts and Donaldson), 1885; archive.org scan antenicenefathers01robe
what_it_says: Irenaeus's rule of faith in English: one God the Father Almighty, one Christ Jesus the Son of God, and the Holy Spirit who proclaimed the economies through the prophets.
limits: English text layer of the Lura-recoded PDF is OCR and is interleaved with the bracketed editorial insertions; the phrase '[She believes]' is the translator's. The quoted English omits the Latin/Greek notes.

ref: 2.28.5 (ANF section 5 of Book II ch. 28; the brief's '2.13.8' is not this passage)
greek: in eo autem qui sit super omnes Deus, totus Nus et totus Logos cum sit, quemadmodum preediximus, et nec aliud antiquius
greek_edition: Latin, Harvey 1857 vol. 1 p. 285 (PDF p. 484; running head 'NON VERBO AUT VITA ANTECEDIT. 285'), Tesseract OCR of the page image (the sentence is in the OCR text; Latin spelling as read, 'preediximus' is OCR-read).
english: But God being all Mind, and all Logos, both speaks exactly what He thinks, and thinks exactly what He speaks. For His thought is Logos, and Logos is Mind, and Mind comprehending all things is the Father Himself. (ANF text layer, p. 400; see I9-05)
translator: English: W. H. Rambaut (groundwork), revised under Alexander Roberts, ANF vol. 1
edition: Sancti Irenaei ... libros quinque adversus haereses, ed. W. Wigan Harvey, vol. 1, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (archive.org sanctiirenilibr01irengoog; image PDF, OCR only)
what_it_says: God is 'all Mind and all Logos' (totus Nus et totus Logos), so Mind, Logos and the Father are not separate beings; the sentence argues against the Valentinian emission scheme.
limits: Irenaeus's point is about the simplicity of God (not a Trinitarian formula); it does not by itself settle the relation of Son and Spirit to the Father. Some scholars read Logos here as a divine faculty.

ref: 2.28.5 (ANF Book II ch. XXVIII; the sentence is in section 5 printed as '5.')
english: But God being all Mind, and all Logos, both speaks exactly what He thinks, and thinks exactly what He speaks. For His thought is Logos, and Logos is Mind, and Mind comprehending all things is the Father Himself.
translator: English: W. H. Rambaut (groundwork), revised under Alexander Roberts, ANF vol. 1
edition: The Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1 (ed. Roberts and Donaldson), 1885; archive.org scan antenicenefathers01robe
what_it_says: God is all Mind and all Logos; Logos is Mind, and Mind is the Father himself.
limits: Against Gnostic emission; the sentence speaks of God's Mind and Logos generally and does not by itself describe the Son as a distinct person, so it is weak evidence for a Trinitarian reading on its own.

ref: 2.28.6 (ANF section 6 of Book II ch. XXVIII; Mark 13:32)
english: ...the Father alone knows the very day and hour of judgment, when He plainly declares, 'But of that day and that hour knoweth no man, neither the Son, but the Father only.' ... the Son was not ashamed to ascribe the knowledge of that day to the Father only
translator: English: W. H. Rambaut (groundwork), revised under Alexander Roberts, ANF vol. 1
edition: The Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1 (ed. Roberts and Donaldson), 1885; archive.org scan antenicenefathers01robe
what_it_says: Irenaeus cites Mark 13:32 ('neither the Son, but the Father only') and says the Son ascribed that knowledge to the Father, which the Gnostics should not be ashamed to accept either.
limits: Arians and Unitarians cite this as proof that the Son is ignorant and so lower than the Father. Irenaeus's reply is about the Father's authority over the day of judgment, not an admission of ignorance in the Son's divine nature; the reply is brief and does not discuss the human/divine distinction in Christ.

greek: quandoquidem et Dominus, ipse Filius Dei, ipsum judicii diem et horam concessit scire solum Patrem, manifeste dicens: De die autem illa, et hora nemo scit, neque Filius, nisi Pater solus.
greek_edition: Latin, Harvey 1857 vol. 1, Google djvu OCR text only (archive.org sanctiirenilibr01irengoog_djvu.txt). The PDF page is NOT pinned: Tesseract OCR of PDF pp. 484-488 did not return this sentence.
translator: Latin: Harvey 1857 (own OCR reading; no translation)
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 1, Book II ch. 28 (printed page not pinned; ch. begins p. 285)
edition: Sancti Irenaei ... libros quinque adversus haereses, ed. W. Wigan Harvey, vol. 1, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (archive.org sanctiirenilibr01irengoog; image PDF, OCR only)
what_it_says: Irenaeus states that the Lord himself, the Son of God, gave the Father alone knowledge of the day and hour (Mark 13:32).
limits: Page not pinned and text is OCR only; treat as a text witness, not a page-verified quote.

ref: 3.6.1 (Harvey running head 'PRAEDICATIO SPIRITUS'; Latin of the Psalm 82 quotation)
greek: Utrosque enim Dei appellatione signavit Spiritus, et eum qui ungitur Filium, et eum qui ungit, id est Patrem. Et iterum: Deus stetit in synagoga Deorum, in medio autem deos discernit; de Patre, et Filio, et de his qui adoptionem perceperunt, dicit:
greek_edition: Latin, Harvey 1857 vol. 2 (archive.org 10606565bsb), text layer read by pdftotext; printed page verified by running head 'PRAEDICATIO SPIRITUS. 21'
edition: Harvey 1857, vol. 2 (archive.org 10606565bsb; errata page 'Vol. II' seen in pdf p.11; text layer present)
what_it_says: The Spirit calls both the Father and the Son by the title God, and Irenaeus quotes Psalm 82:1 ('God stood in the congregation of the gods') as applied to the Father and the Son and to those adopted.
limits: Irenaeus applies Ps 82 to the Father, the Son and the adopted together; opponents (Unitarians) read the 'gods' as creatures. The Latin here is literal and has no Greek of this sentence.

ref: 3.6.1 (ANF; the Psalm 82 passage is in Book III ch. 6)
english: ...God stood in the congregation of the gods ... He judges among the gods. (ANF text layer; the sentence is interleaved with a footnote column, so re-check the page image)
translator: English: W. H. Rambaut (groundwork), revised under Alexander Roberts, ANF vol. 1
edition: The Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1 (ed. Roberts and Donaldson), 1885; archive.org scan antenicenefathers01robe
what_it_says: Psalm 82 'God stood in the congregation of the gods' is applied by Irenaeus to the Father and the Son.
limits: The English is an OCR text layer and partly interleaved; the Latin (I9-08) is the cleaner witness.

ref: 4.6.6 (ANF section 6, Book IV ch. VI; the 'invisible of the Son' sentence)
english: the Father is the invisible of the Son, but the Son the visible of the Father. (ANF text layer, p. 469; see also 4.6 Latin I9-11)
translator: English: W. H. Rambaut (groundwork), revised under Alexander Roberts, ANF vol. 1
edition: The Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1 (ed. Roberts and Donaldson), 1885; archive.org scan antenicenefathers01robe
what_it_says: The Father is invisible to the Son and the Son is visible to the Father, so that the Son makes the invisible Father known.
limits: The Latin sentence of this exact wording was not located in the Harvey text layer; the ANF English is interleaved with the text column. Arians cite the 'Son is the visible' wording as subordination.

ref: 4.6 (Harvey running head 'PATRIS ET FILII'); the Latin sentence on this page is 'invisibilis per visibilem'
greek: incomprehensibilis per comprehensibilem, et invisibilis per visibilem, cum extra eum non sit, sed in sinu Patris exsistat. Deum enim, inquit, nemo vidit unquam, nisi unigenitus Filius Dei, qui est in sinu
greek_edition: Latin, Harvey 1857 vol. 2 (10606565bsb), pdftotext; printed p. 44 (running head 'PATRIS ET FILII. 44' on the page)
edition: Harvey 1857, vol. 2 (archive.org 10606565bsb; errata page 'Vol. II' seen in pdf p.11; text layer present)
what_it_says: The Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, makes the incomprehensible God comprehensible and the invisible Father visible; no one has seen God except the only-begotten Son.
limits: This wording does not literally say 'the Father is the invisible of the Son'; the ANF wording at I9-10 is a separate sentence. Opponents will read the 'visible' as subordination.

ref: 4.20.1 (Harvey Book IV ch. 20, running head 'RERUM OMNIUM CREATORIS')
greek: Nec enim indigebat horum Deus ad faciendum quae ipse apud se praefinierat fieri, quasi ipse suas non haberet manus. Adest enim ei semper Verbum et Sapientia, Filius et Spiritus, per quos, et in quibus omnia libere et sponte fecit
greek_edition: Latin, Harvey 1857 vol. 2 (10606565bsb), pdftotext; printed p. 213 (running head 'RERUM OMNIUM CREATORIS. 213')
edition: Harvey 1857, vol. 2 (archive.org 10606565bsb; errata page 'Vol. II' seen in pdf p.11; text layer present)
what_it_says: God needed no help to make things: the Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, were always with him, and through them he made all things freely.
limits: The 'two hands' image here is the Word and Wisdom (Son and Spirit); the Latin says 'Sapientia' not 'Spiritus' in this sentence, so the identification of Wisdom with the Spirit is made in 4.20.3 and is what opponents dispute.

english: ...as if He did not possess His own hands. For with Him were always present the Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, by whom and in whom...
translator: English: W. H. Rambaut (groundwork), revised under Alexander Roberts, ANF vol. 1
edition: The Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1 (ed. Roberts and Donaldson), 1885; archive.org scan antenicenefathers01robe
what_it_says: God needed no intermediary 'hands' to make things: the Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, were always present with him in creating.
limits: The 'hands' language is ANF/Latin image; the Word-Wisdom pairing is what Arian and Unitarian critics say confuses Son and Spirit.

greek: Et quoniam Verbum, id est Filius, semper cum Patre erat, per multa demonstravimus. Quoniam autem et Sapientia, quae est Spiritus, erat apud eum ante omnem constitutionem, Prov. ii 19, per Salomonem ait: Deus sapientia fundavit terram
greek_edition: Latin, Harvey 1857 vol. 2 (10606565bsb), pdftotext; printed p. 214 (running head 'PER VERBUM ET SAPIENTIAM. 214')
edition: Harvey 1857, vol. 2 (archive.org 10606565bsb; errata page 'Vol. II' seen in pdf p.11; text layer present)
what_it_says: The Word is the Son, always with the Father; Wisdom, which is the Spirit, was with God before creation, citing Proverbs (Wisdom as the Spirit, not as the Son).
limits: This is the passage the brief flags: Irenaeus names Wisdom as the Spirit, while other texts name Wisdom as the Son; Latin 'quae est Spiritus' is read by pdftotext (OCR-like 'zsquee' in the layer, read as quae). The Prov. citation is printed as 'ii 19' but the quotation continues with Prov. viii; check the Harvey note.

ref: Book IV, Harvey running head 'ET BONUS DEUS' (chapter number not fixed; the brief's '4.38.3' is NOT confirmed by this page)
greek: Sapientia igitur precellet Pater super omnem humanam et angelicam sapientiam, quoniam Dominus, et judex, et justus, et dominator super omnes.
greek_edition: Latin, Harvey 1857 vol. 2 (10606565bsb), pdftotext; printed p. 135 (running head 'ET BONUS DEUS. 135')
edition: Harvey 1857, vol. 2 (archive.org 10606565bsb; errata page 'Vol. II' seen in pdf p.11; text layer present)
what_it_says: Irenaeus says the Father surpasses all human and angelic wisdom, because he is Lord, judge, just and ruler of all; wisdom goes with judgment, and God is good as well as judging.
limits: Read as 'the Father surpasses (is above) all wisdom', the sentence can be cited as a subordination text; the English of this passage was not located in the ANF text layer, so the translation is not checked.

ref: Demonstration sec. 3 (Robinson's numbering; the Armenian sections)
english: Now, that we may not suffer ought of this kind, we must needs hold the rule of the faith without deviation, and do the commandments of God, believing in God and fearing Him as Lord and loving Him as Father.
edition: St Irenaeus: The Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching, transl. J. Armitage Robinson, Translations of Christian Literature, Series IV, Oriental Texts, London: SPCK, 1920 (archive.org StIrenaeus, Google scan; text layer present)
what_it_says: The hearer must keep the rule of faith without deviation: believe God, fear him as Lord, and love him as Father.
limits: The text is about the rule of faith, not Christ or the Spirit explicitly; the Armenian (not Greek) is the source, and the translator names the Armenian as the underlying text.

english: Thus then there is shown forth One God, the Father, not made, invisible, creator of all things; above whom there is no other God, and after whom there is no other God. ... Well also does Paul His apostle say: One God, the Father, who is over all and through all and in us all. For over all is the Father; and through all is the Son, for through Him all things were made by the Father; and in us all is the Spirit, who cries Abba Father...
page: Robinson pp. 73-75 (PDF pp. 88-90; sec. 5 p. 73, sec. 6 p. 74, sec. 7 p. 75)
edition: St Irenaeus: The Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching, transl. J. Armitage Robinson, Translations of Christian Literature, Series IV, Oriental Texts, London: SPCK, 1920 (archive.org StIrenaeus, Google scan; text layer present)
what_it_says: One God the Father is over all; the Son is through all and the Spirit is in us all; the Word declares the Spirit and the Spirit the Word, the Son being the prophets' announcer.
limits: The three-fold formula is Pauline (Eph 4:6) and is a 'one God, three agents' scheme: subordinate language ('over all', 'through all') sits beside the Son and Spirit as God; subordinationist readings lean on the 'over all' wording.

english: Now this God is glorified by His Word who is His Son continually, and by the Holy Spirit who is the Wisdom of the Father of all: and the power(s) of these, (namely) of the Word and Wisdom, which are called Cherubim and Seraphim, with unceasing voices glorify God
edition: St Irenaeus: The Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching, transl. J. Armitage Robinson, Translations of Christian Literature, Series IV, Oriental Texts, London: SPCK, 1920 (archive.org StIrenaeus, Google scan; text layer present)
what_it_says: The Word, who is the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who is the Wisdom of the Father, are the glorifiers of God, and their 'powers' are the Cherubim and Seraphim.
limits: Here Wisdom is identified with the Spirit again, as in 4.20.3; the translation has the Armenian's own parenthetical '(s)' and its notes are omitted.

english: So then the Father is Lord and the Son is Lord, and the Father is God and the Son is God; for that which is begotten of God is God. ... And again David says: The Lord said unto my Lord: Sit on my right hand ... And again Isaiah the prophet says: Thus saith the Lord God to my Anointed the Lord whose right hand I have held, that the Gentiles should hearken before him.
page: Robinson pp. 112-113 (PDF pp. 127-128; sec. 47-48 p. 112; sec. 49 p. 113 inferred from the running head, the page number is not OCR-readable)
edition: St Irenaeus: The Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching, transl. J. Armitage Robinson, Translations of Christian Literature, Series IV, Oriental Texts, London: SPCK, 1920 (archive.org StIrenaeus, Google scan; text layer present)
what_it_says: The Father and the Son are each Lord and God; what is begotten of God is God, and the Son is God by generation, shown by David's and Isaiah's words.
limits: Robinson's footnote cross-refers the 'begotten of God is God' idea to Against Heresies I (note 'I, i. 18'); the Demonstration is in the Armenian only, so this is a translated, not a Greek, witness; Arians read 'begotten' as created.
